Motivated by these challenges, in this paper, we propose a probabilistic safety certificate for latent risk. Our key technical enabler is the application of probabilistic invariance: It relaxes the strict observability requirements imposed by set-invariance methods that demand the knowledge of risk-critical states. The proposed techniques provide linear action constraints that confine the latent risk probability within tolerance. Such constraints can be integrated into model predictive controllers or embedded in data-driven policies to mitigate latent risks. The proposed method is tested using the CARLA simulator and compared with a few existing techniques. The theoretical and empirical analysis jointly demonstrate that the proposed methods assure long-term safety in real-time control in occluded environments without being overly conservative and with transparency to exposed risks.
item.dc:creator: Zhuoyuan Wang, Tongyao Jia, Pharuj Rajborirug, Neeraj Ramesh, Hiroyuki Okuda, Tatsuya Suzuki, Soummya Kar, Yorie Nakahira

item.title: From Inference to Control: Structure-Guided Control of Hypergraph Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2511.08647v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Controllability determines whether a system's state can be guided toward any desired configuration, making it a fundamental prerequisite for designing effective control strategies. In the context of networked systems, controllability is a well-established concept. However, many real-world systems, from biological collectives to engineered infrastructures, exhibit higher-order interactions that cannot be captured by simple graphs. Moreover, the interaction structures might be unknown and difficult to measure directly. Here, we close this gap by combining hypergraph inference with the identification of controllable nodes. Building on the inferred structure, we design a controller that, given a set of controllable nodes, steers the system toward a desired configuration. We formulate analytical controllability guarantees for polynomial systems. For non-polynomial dynamics on hypergraphs, we propose a heuristic method for identifying controllable nodes and validate the proposed approach using Kuramoto oscillators.
item.dc:creator: Robin Delabays, Can Chen, Florian D\"orfler, Yuanzhao Zhang, Giulia De Pasquale

item.title: An Exact Solution Algorithm for the Bi-Level Optimization Problem of Electric Vehicles Charging Station Placement
item.description: arXiv:2511.19884v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This work addresses electric vehicle (EV) charging station placement through a bi-level optimization model, where the upper-level planner maximizes charging revenue by selecting station locations under budget constraints, while EV users at the lower level choose routes and charging stations to minimize travel and charging costs. To account for battery range limitation, we construct a battery-expanded network and apply a shortest path algorithm with Frank-Wolfe traffic assignment. Our primary contribution is developing the first global solution algorithm for large scale EV charging station placement problems. We propose a Branch-and-Price-and-Cut algorithm enhanced with value function cuts and column generation. Our exact algorithm delivers solutions provably within the reported optimality gap of the global optimum with mathematical certainty. Computational experiments on the Eastern Massachusetts network (74 nodes, 248 links), the Anaheim network (416 nodes, 914 links), and the Barcelona network (110 zones, 1,020 nodes, and 2,512 links) demonstrate exceptional performance. Our algorithm terminates in a reasonable runtime while achieving optimality gaps below 1% across all instances. Controlled benchmarks against two genetic algorithms on identical instances confirm that the proposed algorithm finds equal or better solutions in less computation time across all tested networks. The algorithm successfully handles problems with over 300,000 feasible combinations, transforming EV charging infrastructure planning into a tractable optimization suitable for practical decision making on real-world networks with optimality guaranteed.
item.dc:creator: Mobina Nankali, Michael W. Levin

item.title: Braess' Paradoxes in Coupled Power and Transportation Systems
item.description: arXiv:2512.12197v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Transportation electrification introduces strong coupling between the power and transportation systems. In this paper, we generalize the classical notion of Braess' paradox to coupled power and transportation systems, and examine how the cross-system coupling induces new types of Braess' paradoxes. To this end, we model the power and transportation networks as graphs, coupled with charging points connecting to nodes in both graphs. The power system operation is characterized by the economic dispatch optimization, while the transportation system user equilibrium models travelers' route and charging choices. By analyzing simple coupled systems, we demonstrate that capacity expansion in either the transportation or the power system can deteriorate the performance of both systems, and uncover the fundamental mechanisms for such new Braess' paradoxes to occur. We also provide necessary and sufficient conditions for the occurrence of Braess' paradoxes in general coupled systems, leading to managerial insights for infrastructure planners. For general networks, by characterizing generalized user equilibria of coupled systems, we develop charging-pricing policies to mitigate Braess' paradoxes.
item.dc:creator: Minghao Mou, Junjie Qin

item.title: HyperKKL: Enabling Non-Autonomous State Estimation through Dynamic Weight Conditioning
item.description: arXiv:2602.22630v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper proposes HyperKKL, a novel learning approach for designing Kazantzis-Kravaris/Luenberger (KKL) observers for non-autonomous nonlinear systems. While KKL observers offer a rigorous theoretical framework by immersing nonlinear dynamics into a stable linear latent space, its practical realization relies on solving Partial Differential Equations (PDE) that are analytically intractable. Current existing learning-based approximations of the KKL observer are mostly designed for autonomous systems, failing to generalize to driven dynamics without expensive retraining or online gradient updates. HyperKKL addresses this by employing a hypernetwork architecture that encodes the exogenous input signal to instantaneously generate the parameters of the KKL observer, effectively learning a family of immersion maps parameterized by the external drive. We rigorously evaluate this approach against a curriculum learning strategy that attempts to generalize from autonomous regimes via training heuristics alone. The novel approach is illustrated on four numerical simulations in benchmark examples including the Duffing, Van der Pol, Lorenz, and R\"ossler systems.
item.dc:creator: Yahia Salaheldin Shaaban, Salem Lahlou, Abdelrahman Sayed Sayed

item.title: Robust Hybrid Finite-Time Parameter Estimation Without Persistence of Excitation
item.description: arXiv:2603.02534v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper, we consider the problem of estimating parameters of a linear regression model. Using a hybrid systems framework, a hybrid algorithm is proposed allowing the estimate to converge to the exact value of the unknown parameters in predetermined finite time. Interestingly, we show that for the case of constant parameters, the convergence property of the hybrid algorithm holds while only requiring the regressor to be exciting on a given interval. For the case of piecewise constant parameters, the classical persistency of excitation condition is required to guarantee the convergence. Robustness of the proposed algorithm with respect to measurements noise is analysed. Finally, illustrative examples are provided showing the merits of the proposed approach in terms of scalability and the applicability for the general class of time-varying unknown parameters
item.dc:creator: Adnane Saoud, Ryan S. Johnson, Ricardo G. Sanfelice

item.title: Stable Inversion of Discrete-Time Linear Periodically Time-Varying Systems via Cyclic Reformulation
item.description: arXiv:2603.23147v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Inverse systems for discrete-time linear periodically time-varying (LPTV) plants are fundamental to feedforward control and iterative learning control of multirate and periodic systems. Building on the classical cyclic reformulation, which converts an N-periodic system into an equivalent LTI system at the original sampling rate, this paper derives an explicit closed-form N-periodic state-space realization of the inverse for an arbitrary uniform periodic relative degree r >= 0 (defined through the periodic Markov parameters). The technical basis is a structure-preservation property: after absorbing a phase shift for r >= 1, the LTI inverse of the cycled plant provably retains the cyclic (block-circulant/block-diagonal) structure, so that the periodic inverse matrices can be read off block-by-block, in exact correspondence with the LTI inverse. The resulting inverse system is real-valued, causal for r = 0 and r-step-delayed for r >= 1, operates at the original sampling rate, and reconstructs the input exactly under matched initial conditions, with geometric error decay otherwise. Through this correspondence, its stability is shown to be equivalent to the invariant zeros of the cycled plant - the periodic invariant zeros of the plant - lying in the open unit disk, which generalizes the minimum phase condition of the LTI case and is verifiable on a single constant matrix pencil. Numerical examples illustrate the construction, the stability characterization, and the implementation as an online periodic filter.
item.dc:creator: Hiroshi Okajima

item.title: Dynamic Quantum-Assisted Co-Design of Controller and Lyapunov Candidate Parameters for Nonlinear Systems
item.description: arXiv:2605.04296v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper proposes a dynamic quantum-assisted co-design framework for nonlinear closed-loop systems in which controller parameters and Lyapunov candidate parameters are redesigned jointly at successive decision epochs. Unlike conventional nonlinear control designs that typically tune controller gains offline and perform stability analysis separately, the proposed method embeds performance improvement and sample-based Lyapunov verification within a unified online optimization loop. The main novelty is a two-step computational structure that first contracts the continuous admissible search region around the current operating condition using a Black-Hole calibration procedure and then constructs a finite binary representation only over this calibrated region. The encoded objective is obtained from sampled nonlinear closed-loop evaluations and approximated by a local quadratic pseudo-Boolean surrogate, enabling an Ising-type Hamiltonian representation suitable for quantum-assisted optimization. Quantum imaginary time evolution is then used to explore the encoded Hamiltonian, and the resulting candidate bitstrings are decoded into continuous controller and Lyapunov parameters. To reduce dependence on the surrogate model, the decoded candidates are re-evaluated using the original nonlinear closed-loop cost and Lyapunov penalties before the final update is applied. The framework can accommodate sampled forms of different Lyapunov decay specifications by modifying the corresponding penalty and is numerically evaluated on first-order nonlinear consensus, second-order nonlinear consensus, and induction motor drive control examples. The implementation code used to generate the reported results is available at \href{https://github.com/LSU-RAISE-LAB/DQCLS-NS}{GitHub}.
item.dc:creator: Milad Hasanzadeh, Amin Kargarian, Mehdi Farasat

item.title: An integrated interpretable control effectiveness learning and nonlinear control allocation methodology for overactuated aircraft
item.description: arXiv:2606.13794v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Nonlinear dynamics and the strong couplings that arise between multiple effectors undermine the assumptions behind conventional, linear control allocation techniques. When flight enters regimes where nonlinear effects dominate, linear allocators exhibit reduced accuracy due to increased model mismatch, which subsequently degrades performance and robustness of the flight control system. High fidelity onboard models and black box data driven approaches can recover accuracy across the flight envelope, but respectively impose computational burdens prohibitive for real time allocation and sacrifice the interpretability required for verification and fault diagnosis. This paper addresses these limitations by learning an explicit, physics constrained analytical model of the control effectiveness mapping from representative flight data using Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics. The resulting mapping is compact, interpretable, and admits analytical derivatives, enabling efficient computation within nonlinear solvers that additionally incorporate actuator dynamics, without requiring an onboard model. An online adaptation mechanism monitors prediction residuals and refreshes the model when significant plant changes are detected, providing graceful reconfiguration under actuator failures and varying operating conditions. The methodology is evaluated on a high fidelity nonlinear benchmark aircraft across a range of aggressive maneuvers, achieving accuracy comparable to a full nonlinear onboard model while substantially reducing computational cost relative to established baselines.
item.dc:creator: Umut Demir, Aamir Ahmad, Torbj{\o}rn Cunis, Walter Fichter

item.title: Cyclic Reformulation-Based Identification and Polytopic Uncertainty Modeling for Multirate Systems
item.description: arXiv:2607.09194v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Modern control systems increasingly rely on heterogeneous sensors operating at different sampling rates, where intermittently missing outputs pose fundamental challenges for system identification. This paper proposes a non-iterative, control-oriented identification method for multirate systems based on cyclic reformulation. The method transforms multirate data into an expanded time-invariant representation and yields M parameter sets from a single input-output dataset, where M is the least common multiple of the sensor sampling periods. These parameter sets, expressed in a common state coordinate of the original dimension, are used in two complementary ways: their centroid, in which each output row is averaged over the phases at which that output is observed, serves as a noise-reduced nominal model, while their convex hull gives a polytopic uncertainty model whose vertices can be used directly in vertex-based LMI robust control design. Building on the exact cyclic-structure recovery established in the authors' preceding work, the paper contributes the centroid and polytopic models and evaluates them under finite noise through output-level validation statistics. Numerical simulations support both models: an illustrative SISO example shows that the centroid attains higher validation FIT than the best individual vertex and substantially outperforms an interpolation-based baseline, while a MIMO multirate sensing example confirms that the constructed polytope contains models whose validation FIT exceeds 95% on average even at the highest tested noise level. The resulting polytope is a data-derived uncertainty description obtained from a single experiment, so that the framework links multirate system identification with robust-control-oriented uncertainty modeling without iterative EM-type optimization.
item.dc:creator: Hiroshi Okajima, Kakeru Ono

item.title: WULPUS PRO: Multi-mode Ultra-Low-Power Wearable Ultrasound and Array Imaging with CMUT Support
item.description: arXiv:2607.12137v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Wearable ultrasound enables continuous monitoring of physiological processes such as muscle dynamics, bladder volume, and cardiovascular activity. Existing fully wearable ultra-low-power platforms are limited to shallow, low-channel A-mode sensing, while larger multi-mode systems are too bulky and power-hungry for true wearability. We present WULPUS PRO, a runtime-programmable wearable ultrasound acquisition platform measuring $39\times21\times6 \mathrm{mm}$ and weighing $5 \mathrm{g}$. It integrates $30 \mathrm{V}$ excitation, 16 time-multiplexed channels, a low-noise receive front-end with up to $70 \mathrm{dB}$ gain, $14 \mathrm{MHz}$ bandwidth, time-gain compensation, and $45 \mathrm{dB}$ SNR. The platform supports deep-tissue echo acquisition up to $2.2 \mathrm{MHz}$ in RF-sampling mode and $8 \mathrm{MHz}$ in envelope-detection mode. We demonstrate B-mode imaging in a 16-channel ultra-low-power wearable with sub-millimeter axial and millimeter-scale lateral resolution in phantom experiments, while consuming $40 \mathrm{mW}$ at $50 \mathrm{Hz}$ PRF and under $60 \mathrm{mW}$ at $300 \mathrm{Hz}$ PRF. WULPUS PRO supports both piezoelectric and capacitive micromachined ultrasonic transducers, enabling integration with skin-conformal polymer-based CMUT arrays. As a host-agnostic acquisition front-end, it exposes standard data and power interfaces for BLE- and Wi-Fi-based wearable hosts. We demonstrate wireless transmission with external BLE and Wi-Fi modules and project 1-2 days of BLE operation at $50 \mathrm{Hz}$ PRF and over 3 h of Wi-Fi streaming at $300 \mathrm{Hz}$ PRF using a $300 \mathrm{mAh}$, $6.4 \mathrm{g}$ Li-Po cell. WULPUS PRO establishes a new class of fully programmable, B-mode-enabled, ultra-low-power wearable ultrasound platforms.
item.dc:creator: Sergei Vostrikov, Federico Villani, Cedric Hirschi, Jinhao Lu, Jonas Welsch, Martin Angerer, Edmond Cretu, Robert Rohling, Andrea Cossettini, Luca Benini

item.title: Dynamic Constraint Reconstruction Based Control Barrier Functions for Safety-Critical Control of High-Dimensional Manipulators
item.description: arXiv:2607.15961v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Control barrier functions (CBFs) provide formal safety guarantees for constrained nonlinear systems, but their effectiveness relies on accurate system dynamics. In high-dimensional manipulators subject to unknown disturbances and model uncertainties, fixed safety constraints constructed from nominal dynamics may become inconsistent with the actual system behavior, leading to safety degradation or excessive conservatism. This paper proposes a dynamic constraint reconstruction based control barrier function (DCR-CBF) framework for safety-critical control of disturbed robotic manipulators. An extended state observer is employed to estimate lumped disturbances online, and the estimated disturbance is incorporated into high-order control barrier functions to reconstruct safety constraints according to the estimated true dynamics. To address estimation inaccuracies, a safety margin is introduced, and a sufficient condition is derived to guarantee forward invariance under bounded estimation errors. Simulation studies on a 4-DOF excavation manipulator demonstrate that the proposed DCR-CBF method achieves zero safety violation under strong unknown disturbances while significantly improving trajectory-tracking performance compared with standard and robust CBF methods.
item.dc:creator: Bingsheng Zhang, Shen Wang, Qiang Wang, Muguo Du, Donghai Shi, Xiaofeng Tao

item.title: A Hierarchical Optimisation Framework for Integrated Electric-Hydrogen-Transport Systems
item.description: arXiv:2607.25776v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Integrated electric-hydrogen infrastructures are becoming increasingly important with the growing deployment of electric vehicles (EVs) and hydrogen vehicles (HVs) in transport systems. However, the strong coupling between vehicle scheduling and multi-energy dispatch introduces significant operational challenges. This paper models an integrated electric-hydrogen-transport system (EHTS) and proposes a hierarchical optimisation framework that couples vehicle scheduling and downstream energy dispatch through a sequential, demand-driven two-layer structure. In the vehicle scheduling layer, a solver-free greedy heuristic (SFGH) algorithm is developed to avoid repeated optimisation solving, enabling real-time EV charging and HV refuelling under non-preemptive service and within-interval sequential assignment. The resulting charging and refuelling demands are subsequently passed to the energy dispatch layer, where a deep reinforcement learning (DRL)-based approach is designed to optimise battery operation, hydrogen-tank operation, and PV generation allocation to minimise the overall operational cost of the EHTS while satisfying the scheduled transport demand. Representative case studies, together with comparative, ablation, and generalisation analyses, demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed framework. Furthermore, the learned dispatch policy maintains strong performance across diverse transport-demand scenarios and PV penetration levels without retraining, demonstrating robust generalisation capability for practical deployment.
item.dc:creator: Fulong Yao, Yiming Xu, Liana Cipcigan, Maurizio Albano, Naeima Hamed, Nima Valizadeh, Omer Rana

item.title: Analytical Prediction of Voltage Collapse in Current-Limited Grid-Forming Inverters
item.description: arXiv:2608.04740v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As converter-interfaced units become dominant in power systems, understanding nonlinear stability phenomena involving discrete switching events becomes essential for secure operation. The limited overcurrent capability of grid-forming (GFM) inverters makes current limiting essential during large disturbances. Activation of a circular current limiter (CCL) can cause the operating equilibrium to disappear under certain circumstances. This paper develops an analytical framework to predict the grid-voltage boundaries for CCL activation and determine whether the operating equilibrium persists or disappears after activation. For CCL-based GFM inverters with frozen anti-windup, closed-form expressions for the activation boundaries are derived while accounting for the filter capacitor. A criterion is established to determine whether a saturated (i.e., current-limited) stable equilibrium point (satSEP) persists following limiter activation. A continuation method is also developed to trace equilibria across normal-control and current-limited operation. Power-angle analysis and dynamic-model continuation in single-inverter and modified 9-bus systems validate these predictions. Time-domain simulations further confirm the results. The results show that CCL activation can either cause immediate loss of the stable equilibrium or allow stable current-limited operation to continue until the equilibrium is lost as operating conditions change further.
item.dc:creator: Wenhao Lin, Robin Preece, Panagiotis N. Papadopoulos

item.title: Reduced Arc-Weight Heterogeneity for Master Stability Analysis of Directed Networks
item.description: arXiv:2608.14439v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Master stability analysis can be applied to directed networks even when their Laplacian matrices are not diagonalizable. Nevertheless, a diagonalizable Laplacian is easier to analyse because the perturbations governing synchronization separate into independent modes. This paper asks how many different positive coupling strengths are needed to obtain this simplification without adding or removing any directed connections. We first give an elementary construction showing that suitable positive weights exist for every weakly connected directed network and explain its relationship to stronger genericity results in the literature. We then introduce a measure of the smallest number of distinct coupling strengths required for diagonalizability. If a common coupling strength already produces a diagonalizable Laplacian, only one value is needed. For directed acyclic networks, we give a constructive upper bound based on the length of the longest directed path from a source. This bound is exact for rooted outward directed trees. Consequently, an outward star requires only one coupling value, whereas a directed path requires a different value on every arc. These results reduce coupling heterogeneity while retaining the simpler modal form of master stability analysis. Diagonalizability is treated as an analytical convenience, not as a sufficient condition for synchronization.
item.dc:creator: Aandrew Baggio Sahaya Arokiadoss, G. Arunkumar

item.title: A Control Co-Design Framework to Optimize Sustainability with Application to Microgrid-Driven Data Centers
item.description: arXiv:2609.01912v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This work studies the optimization of physical plant characteristics and controller parameters for sustainability. Environmental sustainability is strongly correlated with the development and operation of energy systems, with data centers as the preeminent modern example. Data centers, and the grid technologies that provide their power, consume nonnegligible amounts of global energy and pose a risk to increase greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and electronic waste. Addressing such issues requires improved plant design and control strategies, often approached through optimization-based methods. However, there are noticeable gaps regarding data center and microgrid design: (i) simultaneous optimization of plant and controller features is rarely explored, and (ii) sustainability criteria are not emphasized. This work addresses these gaps by establishing a generalized, sustainability-centric control co-design (CCD) framework for energy systems. Uniquely, the CCD framework defines and categorizes sustainability metrics into three lifecycle stages - manufacturing, operation, and disposal - supporting optimization and comparative analysis of the metrics for different design options. To exemplify its use, the CCD framework is applied to a microgrid-driven data center system, providing a family of sustainability metrics correlated to plant and controller parameters. The analysis enabled by the framework supports the determination of tradeoffs between different types of environmental sustainability metrics. The system designs identified by the proposed framework show substantial improvements to environmental sustainability categories as compared to designs identified through baseline procedures.
item.dc:creator: Tania Rifat Jahan, Donald J. Docimo

item.title: Identifiability-Guided Composite Load Modeling of AI Data Centers
item.description: arXiv:2610.19565v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The rapid growth of AI data centers introduces large, workload-dependent loads whose protection and reconnection behavior can affect power-system transient stability. Calibrating dynamic models of such loads is challenging because treating all associated elements as freely estimable may lead to weakly identified or physically confounded parameterizations. This paper proposes an identifiability-guided calibration framework for a composite load model with separate IT, cooling, and auxiliary branches. A nuisance-projected Fisher-information criterion characterizes the local identifiability of the cooling-motor composition, while a workload non-equivalence result shows that voltage-only recalibration cannot reproduce workload-dependent responses. Guided by these results, a grey-box estimator trained with branch-level supervision learns the workload-to-power relation and the cooling composition, while retaining a prescribed UPS protection law and an externally anchored reconnect-ramp duration. The learned workload relation is then distilled into a closed form for transient-stability simulation. Evaluation using 300,000 MIT Supercloud GPU power-utilization samples and 12,600 IEEE 39-bus fault scenarios yields an aggregate active-power $R^2$ of 0.948, compared with 0.856 for an LSTM baseline. Removing branch-level supervision preserves relatively high aggregate accuracy but substantially degrades cooling-component recovery. Under unseen deep voltage sags, the proposed model achieves a transient $R^2$ of 0.750, compared with 0.033 for the LSTM. Closed-loop simulations further show that cooling composition and protection behavior can affect retained-load states and voltage responses near protection thresholds.
item.dc:creator: Ding Lin, Jianhui Wang, Meng Yue, Tianqiao Zhao

item.title: Physical AI: A Survey of Models, Learning, Systems, and Open Challenges
item.description: arXiv:2610.21171v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Physical AI aims to enable intelligent systems to perceive, reason, act, and learn through interaction with the physical world. Unlike purely digital intelligence, physical agents must operate under partial observability, uncertain dynamics, embodiment constraints, and real-time requirements, while their actions continuously reshape the environment and subsequent observations. Recent advances in foundation models and robot learning have expanded the capabilities of physical agents, yet achieving reliable autonomy requires more than improvements in individual models. This survey presents a comprehensive, system-level review of Physical AI, organized around the closed-loop process of physical interaction. We examine the foundations and recent developments in task representations and memory, predictive and action-generating models, data and learning methods, embodiment and control, computing systems, evaluation, and safety. Beyond reviewing individual advances, we investigate how these components interact and collectively shape the capabilities and limitations of Physical AI systems. Building on this integrated perspective, we identify fundamental challenges in generalization, resource-efficient learning and execution, reliable state tracking, safety, recovery, and continual adaptation. We argue that advancing Physical AI requires moving beyond isolated model performance toward integrated systems capable of robust, efficient, safe, and autonomous physical interaction under changing real-world conditions.
item.dc:creator: Bin Gao, Anuj Gautam, Aritra Bagchi, Yunkai Liang, Wentao Li, Ronghui Zhu, Zhi Zhou, Yancan Mao, Xiao Yan, Xin He, Qingyun Zou, Wenshuo Yue, Dan Chen, Zhanglu Yan, Fei Xu, Huize Li, Weijie Wang, Tao Ouyang, Tulika Mitra

item.title: Provable Bounds on the Hessian of Neural Networks: Derivative-Preserving Reachability Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2406.04476v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We propose a novel reachability analysis method tailored for neural networks with smooth activations. Our method relies on constructing an end-to-end first-order Taylor expansion of the network and bounding the remainder. To enable this, we develop a scalable algorithm for computing closed-form bounds on both the gradient norm and Hessian norm of the network. A key component is a loop transformation of the activation functions, which leverages their monotonicity to sharpen the bounds. This yields a local abstraction that preserves the network's value and gradient at the expansion point. For larger input domains, we integrate this local model into a branch-and-bound scheme, recursively refining the overapproximation. We validate our approach through extensive experiments and demonstrate scalability and accuracy improvements over state-of-the-art verification baselines.
item.dc:creator: Sina Sharifi, Mahyar Fazlyab

item.title: Topological entropy of nonlinear time-varying systems
item.description: arXiv:2509.13537v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the topological entropy of nonlinear time-varying systems. We establish conditions under which entropy is independent of the initial time and derive two general upper bounds based on the matrix measure of the system Jacobian and the spectral abscissa of a Metzler comparison matrix, respectively. A general lower bound is also obtained using the trace of the Jacobian. For interconnected systems, we first derive an upper bound using the matrix measure of an interconnection matrix constructed from the Jacobian blocks. We then establish a new upper bound based on the spectral abscissa of a Metzler comparison matrix, incorporating the interconnection structure through subsystem-wise trajectory-separation analysis. This bound also recovers the two general upper bounds as special cases. All bounds depend on asymptotic properties of the Jacobian over reachable sets or their convex hulls. Simple examples show that either general upper bound may be tighter, while a time-varying Lorenz system illustrates the effects of norm selection and subsystem decomposition.
item.dc:creator: Guosong Yang, Daniel Liberzon

item.title: Quotient Geometry and Persistence-Stable Metrics for Swarm Configurations
item.description: arXiv:2603.18041v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Can temporal information recover geometry lost by a persistence diagram? For $n\ge3$ points on the unit sphere evolving under known homogeneous complete consensus, we prove generic local recovery modulo rotations and permutations from two ordinary zero-dimensional Vietoris--Rips persistence snapshots. The structural result applies to every labeled tree: its edge inner products and their first temporal derivatives have differential rank $2n-3$, exactly the dimension of the regular formation quotient. An explicit pole--equator witness proves this simultaneously for all tree types after taking a finite intersection of open dense sets. Although one snapshot has generic local fibers of dimension $n-2$, two sufficiently close snapshots are injective on a common neighborhood. The optimal inverse Lipschitz constant grows as $\Theta(1/|h|)$ when the sampling interval tends to zero. A verified left inverse, interval derivative bounds, and explicit persistence-matching margins certify neighborhoods and time intervals at rational reference formations. The results are local and model-specific; reflection ambiguity and centered rank obstructions remain.
item.dc:creator: Mark M. Bailey

item.title: When is cumulative dose response monotonic? Analysis of incoherent feedforward motifs
item.description: arXiv:2604.01573v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the monotonicity of the cumulative dose response (cDR) for a class of incoherent feedforward motifs (IFFM) systems with linear intermediate dynamics and nonlinear output dynamics. While the instantaneous dose response (DR) may be nonmonotone with respect to the input, the cDR can still be monotone. To analyze this phenomenon, we derive an integral representation of the sensitivity of cDR with respect to the input and establish general sufficient conditions for both monotonicity and nonmonotonicity. These results reduce the problem to verifying qualitative sign properties along system trajectories. The structural conditions identify eight canonical IFFM models, four of which are analyzed in detail within the proposed framework. In particular, IFFM1 and IFFM3 exhibit monotone cDR despite potentially nonmonotone DR, while IFFM2 is monotone already at the level of DR, which implies monotonicity of cDR. In contrast, IFFM4 exhibits nonmonotone cDR. Numerical simulations indicate that these properties persist beyond the structured initial conditions used in the analysis. Overall, our results provide a unified framework for understanding how system structure shapes monotonicity in cumulative input--output responses.

item.title: Rate-Cost Tradeoffs in Nonlinear Control
item.description: arXiv:2604.20369v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study finite-horizon rate-cost tradeoffs for general stochastic control systems, including nonlinear systems. Under an average control cost constraint, we show that the minimum expected communication rate lies within an additive logarithmic gap above the normalized directed information minimized over causal control policies. This establishes directed information as the operationally relevant quantity governing rate-limited control, extending its previously established roles in causal source coding and linear quadratic Gaussian (LQG) control to general nonlinear control systems.
item.dc:creator: Eray Unsal Atay, Venkat Chandrasekaran, Victoria Kostina

item.title: MIRA: A Modular Open-Source Micro-UAV for Indoor Research
item.description: arXiv:2607.11785v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Indoor robotics research increasingly relies on micro-UAV platforms whose airframes, electronics, and control software are open to modification. Off-the-shelf platforms often lack the low-level access that such modifications require, while building a custom vehicle demands substantial engineering effort before the first flight test, leaving many laboratories working within constraints that limit the scope of their research. We present MIRA (Modular Indoor Research Architecture), an open-source micro-UAV for indoor research, built around a replicable 3D-printed PLA airframe with detachable arms and a containerized low-level software package that manages the companion-to-autopilot communication bridge via Micro XRCE-DDS. Designed as a white-box architecture, its core subsystems, including the companion computer, are individually replaceable without firmware refactoring, which supports local fabrication, crash-localized repair, and component substitution from existing laboratory inventory. We characterize MIRA through autonomous flights comprising takeoff, hovering, trajectory tracking, and landing within an optical motion-capture volume. The communication pipeline sustains a median companion-to-autopilot latency of 0.02 ms, with the external motion-capture link as the main remaining latency source, and time-domain analysis shows that structural vibration remains stable during dynamic maneuvers and below the reference level adopted in this work. All design files and software are released openly to support replication and extension by other laboratories.

item.title: Mode-Weighted Transport Certificates for State-Dependent Reflected Switching Diffusions
item.description: arXiv:2608.01992v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: State-dependent switching diffusions can contract in law even when individual modes are expansive. We establish a computable, constant-one contraction certificate on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and compact convex domains with normal reflection. The mode-weighted transport cost combines spatial separation with a discrete graph penalty and retains spatial dependence when the modes differ. A synchronous Brownian coupling and a maximal coupling of jump clocks in equal modes lead to separate equal- and unequal-mode generator inequalities. We give a complete regularization argument for the nonsmooth cost, including the drift and jump errors, the sign of reflection, and the limiting It\^o-Dynkin calculation. A resolvent proof transfers contraction to probability-valued weak solutions of the no-flux Fokker-Planck-Kolmogorov system, while an explicit Foster-Lyapunov condition ensures existence and uniqueness of an invariant law on the whole space. For fixed weight ordering and decay rate, certificate synthesis is a semi-infinite linear feasibility problem; on compact domains, a Lipschitz-buffered finite mesh provides a rigorous test. One-dimensional and planar examples illustrate the certificate and its numerical verification.
item.dc:creator: Yutong Zhu, Ye Zhang

item.title: Repeated Binary Direct Collinear Impacts Under Incremental Contact Laws With Residual Indentation: A Hybrid Systems Formulation
item.description: arXiv:2609.06138v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Incremental contact laws specify the normal contact force through a differential relation, possibly carrying an internal state, driven by the indentation and its rate. In some, the force is extinguished at a nonzero indentation, whether by plastic deformation or by an elastic aftereffect, so that a residual deformation remains at separation. Such laws sit uneasily within rigid body dynamics, which admits no deformation. The tension is tolerable when the indentation is small relative to the bodies, so that it may be carried constitutively rather than geometrically. Even then, the contact law alone does not determine the interaction of the bodies. Because force and indentation no longer vanish together, conditions for the commencement and termination of contact must be supplied separately. So must the fate of the deformation and internal state at separation, neither of which the equations of motion contain. This article formulates the repeated direct collinear impact of two convex bodies under external forces as a hybrid dynamical system. The contact interface is modeled as a massless element carrying the contact law and its state, coupled to the bodies through relative velocity and an interaction force dictated by the contact state. Consequently, all switching and resets are confined to the interface, leaving the geometry and the equations of motion of the bodies unaltered. The principal analytical properties of the resulting formulations are established, among them passivity and completeness; the branching of solutions at the onset and termination of contact is also examined. The framework is demonstrated through numerical simulations.

item.title: Joint Deployment and Resource Management for Group-Tag-Based Physical-Layer Authentication and Collaborative Communication in NTN
item.description: arXiv:2609.09475v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Physical-layer authentication (PLA) in non-terrestrial networks (NTNs) has primarily been studied from a security perspective, while its system-level integration with communication remains less explored. We propose the secure adaptive framework for authentication in multi-zone networks (SAFA-MZ), a system-level formulation for the joint management of collaborative group-tag and private-data delivery in NTN, where high-altitude platform station (HAPS) placement, user association, and transmission powers are jointly selected under service and secrecy constraints. Group-level authentication tags and user data are collaboratively transmitted by multiple HAPSs, with artificial noise (AN) mitigating information leakage. We jointly optimize HAPS placement, user association, and power allocation to balance deployment regularity, tag distribution, and user-rate fairness under secrecy, quality-of-service (QoS), power, and coverage constraints. The problem is addressed using a repair-based cross-entropy method (RCEM) and a graph-aware advantage actor-critic (A2C) algorithm (GA2C). Under colluding and non-colluding eavesdropper models, GA2C improves average secrecy spectral efficiency (SSE) by 135--139% over its single-connect baseline and 21.1--23.2% over its baseline without AN. Across ten independent random seeds, GA2C achieves approximately 23.4% and 17.9% higher mean per-user SSE under non-colluding and colluding eavesdropping, respectively, and a 16.2\% higher mean private-rate Jain's index than RCEM. These results quantify the gains of multi-node connectivity and AN within the proposed framework under the evaluated assumptions.

item.title: From Optical Flow to Safety: Visual Safety Certification via Scale-Free Relative Motion
item.description: arXiv:2610.21374v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Safe autonomous navigation using monocular vision remains challenging because explicit obstacle states are not directly observable. This letter introduces a visual safety-certification paradigm that uses scale-free, depth-normalized relative motion encoded by monocular optical flow as the representation for collision-risk certification, without reconstructing obstacle position, velocity, geometry, or a metric world model. Unlike conventional optical-flow-based navigation approaches that rely on image motion to shape avoidance behavior, the proposed framework directly encodes collision-cone geometry and safety constraints in this relative-motion representation. An online Concurrent Learning observer estimates the normalized relative velocity and provides a computable estimation-error bound. This uncertainty is propagated into the collision cone through angular inflation and a monocular robot-footprint margin, yielding a Robust Vision-Based Collision Cone Control Barrier Function (RV-C$^3$BF). An optimal-decay CBF quadratic program minimally modifies the nominal control input to enforce the resulting robust safety constraint under the stated assumptions. Extensive simulation and real-world experiments on a TurtleBot3 in cluttered environments with static and dynamic obstacles demonstrate collision avoidance using only monocular vision and onboard proprioception, with the estimation-error bound containing the measured error in $98.3\%$ of simulation samples and the robot achieving collision-free navigation in $93$ of $100$ real-world trials.

item.title: The role of distributed friction dynamics on heave-induced motion of offshore drilling systems: modelling, analysis, and simulations
item.description: arXiv:2610.22189v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper investigates the influence of friction dynamics on heave-induced disturbance propagation using a coupled hydraulic-structural drilling model formulated as a semilinear interconnection of ordinary and hyperbolic partial differential equations (ODE-PDEs), and capturing spatially distributed memory effects in the drillstring-wellbore interaction. First, local and global existence and uniqueness results are established, and sufficient conditions for boundedness and input-to-state stability are deduced via a small-gain analysis. Subsequently, extensive numerical investigations are carried out, including harmonic excitation studies, nonlinear distortion analysis, spatial amplification investigations, mechanism-isolation experiments, parameter sensitivity analysis, and broadband simulations under realistic offshore sea-state excitation. The simulation results indicate that, whilst the hydraulic response is governed primarily by wave propagation phenomena, compressibility, and boundary reflections, the structural dynamics display substantially greater sensitivity to distributed friction effects. Furthermore, drillstring-wellbore friction is shown to have a relatively limited influence on well-posedness but a potentially significant impact on stability margins. These findings highlight the importance of accounting for coupled hydraulic-structural dynamics and distributed friction mechanisms when analysing, monitoring, and controlling offshore drilling systems.
